text: Alexei Alexeyevich Abrikosov (Russian: Алексе́й Алексе́евич Абрико́сов; June 25, 1928 – March 29, 2017[4][5]) was a Soviet, Russian, and American[6] theoretical physicist known primarily for his work in condensed matter physics. He shared the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physics with Vitaly Ginzburg and Anthony James Leggett for theories explaining how matter behaves at extremely low temperatures.[6][7][8] Born in Moscow, Russian SFSR, Soviet Union, on June 25, 1928, to physicians Aleksey Abrikosov and Fani (née Wulf), Abrikosov was of Jewish descent.[9] After graduating from high school in 1943, he studied energy technology and earned a degree from Moscow State University in 1948. From 1948 to 1965, he worked at the Institute for Physical Problems of the USSR Academy of Sciences, where he received his Ph.D. in 1951 for his work on the theory of thermal diffusion in plasmas and his Doctor of Physical and Mathematical Sciences degree in 1955 for research on quantum electrodynamics at high energies. He moved to the United States in 1991 and resided there until his death in Palo Alto, California, in 2017 at the age of 88.[19] During his time in the U.S., he was elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2000 and became a foreign member of the Royal Society in 2001.[3][10] From 1965 to 1988, he worked at the Landau Institute for Theoretical Physics (USSR Academy of Sciences) and remained a professor at Moscow State University since 1965. He also held tenure at the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology from 1972 to 1976 and at the Moscow Institute of Steel and Alloys from 1976 to 1991. He served as a full member of the USSR Academy of Sciences from 1987 to 1991 and became a full member of the Russian Academy of Sciences in 1991. In 1952 and 1957, Abrikosov published work explaining how magnetic flux can penetrate certain superconductors, leading to the classification of these materials as type-II superconductors, with the resulting pattern of magnetic flux lines known as the Abrikosov vortex lattice.[11] Together with Lev Gor'kov and Igor Dzyaloshinskii, he authored a foundational textbook on theoretical solid-state physics used for decades to train physicists. From 1991 until his retirement, he worked at Argonne National Laboratory in Illinois, where he was an Argonne Distinguished Scientist in the Condensed Matter Theory Group. At the time of receiving the Nobel Prize, his research focused on the origins of magnetoresistance—the property of some materials to change their electrical resistance under a magnetic field.[12][13][14][15][16] He received the Lenin Prize in 1966, the Fritz London Memorial Prize in 1972, the USSR State Prize in 1982, and the Landau Prize from the Russian Academy of Sciences in 1989. In 1991, he was awarded the Sony Corporation's John Bardeen Award and became a Foreign Honorary Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. He was also a member of the Royal Academy of London, a fellow of the American Physical Society, and a recipient of the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physics. His father, Alexey Ivanovich Abrikosov (1875–1955), was a physician, and his mother, Fania Davidovna Woolf (1895–1965), was also a physician; through his father, he was the nephew of the Catholic nun Anna Abrikosova (1882–1936). His sister, Maria Alekseevna Abrikósova (1929–1998), was also a physician. He married Svetlana Yuriyevna Bunkova and had three children.[6][3]
